passage:
Dear Mrs Bhatt,

I'm writing because I can't say this out loud without crying. For about six weeks, Kamal has blocked me in the corridor outside the science lab and pushed my bag off my shoulder. He calls me names and the others laugh. I have told my mother I have a stomach ache four times so I don't have to come to school, but it isn't true. I feel sick when the bell rings. I used to think I must have done something to deserve it. I've started to believe that isn't true. I wrote down the dates: 3, 10 and 17 September, and yesterday. I stay near Anaya and Meher at break, and they don't laugh. Please can we talk after class on Monday? I'd rather not do this alone.

Arohi

Mrs Bhatt's reply, the same afternoon: Thank you for telling me, Arohi. This is not your fault. Stay after the last bell today and we'll see the counsellor together.

qa.q: For about how long has Kamal been blocking Arohi in the corridor?
qa.a: He has been doing it for about six weeks.

qa.q: What is Arohi feeling about school, and how do you know?
qa.a: Dread and fear. Arohi writes of feeling sick when the bell rings and of claiming stomach aches four times to avoid coming.

qa.q: What steps has Arohi taken that a wise person would suggest?
qa.a: Arohi wrote down the dates, stays near supportive friends at break and is asking the teacher for a talk instead of facing it alone.

qa.q: How might Mrs Bhatt feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Probably concerned and glad Arohi trusted her; she replies that same afternoon, says it is not Arohi's fault and arranges to see the counsellor together.

grounding: Arohi dreads the corridor and lies about being sick because of a bully, and writes to a trusted teacher with dates, staying near supportive friends.
